items.title: Slow Zoom In
items.description: A slow zoom in is slow zoom in cinematography that tightens the frame by increasing focal length while the camera body stays locked. Perspective relations stay fixed: the world does not slide, it only enlarges as the lens compresses space.

items.title: Slow Zoom Out
items.description: A slow zoom out widens the frame by decreasing focal length while the support stays put. More architecture and negative space enter the picture, yet the camera never travels, so true parallax does not appear.

items.title: Crash Zoom In
items.description: A crash zoom is a rapid focal-length snap from a wider frame into a detail, usually without moving the camera. The punch is optical and conspicuous: size changes faster than a body can walk.

items.title: Crash Zoom Out
items.description: A crash zoom out is a sudden, fast widening of the lens from a tight frame into a much wider one, usually without moving the camera. It dumps the subject back into the environment in a fraction of a second.

items.title: Dolly In
items.description: A dolly in shot moves the entire camera through space on a wheeled or tracked support, advancing toward the subject at a measured pace. The nodal point walks, so foreground and background shift in parallax as the surroundings are progressively excluded.

items.title: Dolly Out
items.description: A dolly out shot withdraws the entire camera through space on a wheeled or tracked support. The world widens with true parallax, and the subject shrinks inside architecture because the station point has actually retreated.

items.title: Dolly Left
items.description: A dolly left, also called a truck left, slides the whole camera sideways to the left on wheels or track. The lens stays aimed with the subject while background planes peel past in parallax.

items.title: Dolly Right
items.description: A dolly right, or truck right, moves the camera body sideways to the right without panning. New space enters from one side of the frame while the other side exits, and layered parallax proves the translation.

items.title: Pan Left
items.description: A pan left is pan shot cinematography that rotates the camera on a fixed tripod or head around its vertical axis, sweeping the view to the left. The support does not travel; only the direction of the lens changes.

items.title: Pan Right
items.description: A pan right shot is a horizontal rotation of a locked-off camera toward the right. It connects two parts of the same geography in one continuous turn from a single station point.

items.title: Tilt Up
items.description: A tilt up shot rotates the camera vertically around a fixed position, climbing from a lower composition to a higher one. The tripod does not rise; only pitch changes, so the viewpoint height stays the same.

items.title: Tilt Down
items.description: A tilt-down rotates the camera vertically from a fixed position, starting higher and ending lower. It can drop from sky or architecture onto a person or object without moving the tripod.

items.title: Whip Pan
items.description: A whip pan pans so quickly that the image blurs into horizontal streaks, then snaps to a new composition. Two shots can be joined inside compatible directional motion blur, creating the impression of one fast reorientation.

items.title: Whip Tilt
items.description: A whip tilt is a violent, motion-blurred vertical rotation of the camera, then a hard stop. It is the up-or-down cousin of a whip pan: shock through speed, not through traveling the support.

items.title: Pedestal Up
items.description: A pedestal shot moves the entire camera vertically without changing its tilt. The lens rises on a column, eyeline climbs, and architecture slides down the frame while pitch stays constant.

items.title: Pedestal Down
items.description: A pedestal down lowers the entire camera vertically without changing its tilt. The descent stays on one axis: a calm drop through the same look, not a nod and not a crane swoop.

items.title: Crane Up
items.description: A crane shot lifts the camera on a jib or Technocrane, often easing backward at the same time, so the frame climbs from a human scale into a wider view of the location. Height change is the point, and a little boom-out keeps the subject from sliding off the bottom of the frame.

items.title: Crane Down
items.description: A crane down shot lowers the camera on an arm from a high wide view into a human-scale frame. The world collapses from map to face because the lens occupies new heights, not because it merely nods.

items.title: Crane Over
items.description: A crane-over lifts and arcs the camera on a jib or crane until it looks down on the scene from above. Height and angle change together in one move, turning the floor into a map.

items.title: Jib Shot
items.description: A jib shot uses a short pivoting arm to raise, lower, or sweep the camera a few feet. It is a compact crane: small height change, often over a table, a walk, or a two-shot.

items.title: 360-Degree Orbit
items.description: A 360-degree orbit shot circles the subject through a full turn, usually at a constant radius, always facing them. The background becomes a continuous ribbon while the person stays the center of interest.

items.title: Arc Left
items.description: An arc left is a curved dolly that travels partway around the subject while staying aimed at them. The camera's axis on the conversation or room changes without a cut, usually about a quarter-orbit.

items.title: Arc Right
items.description: An arc right is a partial orbit to the right, usually about a quarter turn, with the lens remaining on the subject. Background slides while eyeline and distance stay roughly constant.

items.title: Tracking Shot
items.description: A tracking shot moves with, beside, ahead of, or behind a moving subject, typically matching pace on a parallel path. The person supplies the motion; the camera keeps distance, height, and scale while foreground, mid-ground, and deep background peel.

items.title: Follow Shot
items.description: A follow shot trails a moving subject at a fixed offset, usually from behind. The back of the head becomes foreground and the world opens ahead, so pursuit, haunting, or arrival is felt as walking into space.

items.title: Steadicam
items.description: Steadicam is a mechanical stabilizing system using a sled, arm, and vest, so an operator can walk while the camera floats. The path can connect rooms with a smoothness that is neither handheld tremor nor dolly traction.

items.title: Handheld
aliases: The Children of Men car ambush
items.description: A handheld camera is operated from the body without a stabilizing vest or gimbal, so breathing, micro-shake, and mass stay in the frame. The image has the nerves of a person holding weight, not a track and not a motor.

items.title: Gimbal Shot
items.description: A gimbal shot uses motorized stabilization for smooth handheld or vehicle-mounted movement. Electronic inertia damps roll and high-frequency shake while a human still carries the camera, freer than a dolly and cleaner than raw handheld.

items.title: FPV Drone
items.description: An FPV drone shot is first-person aerial flying: the camera banks, dives, and threads architecture at high speed. It is proximity and flight, a racing craft with a lens, not a slow crane and not a high establishing hover.

items.title: Aerial Pullback
items.description: An aerial pullback rises and recedes until a person or building becomes a small mark in a landscape. The move hands the scene from a character to geography, from helicopter or high-drone height rather than from a ground crane.

items.title: Aerial Push In
items.description: An aerial push in starts high and descends or tightens until a single figure reads in the map. It picks one human out of a city, crowd, or terrain from altitude.

items.title: Push In
items.description: A push in shot moves physically or virtually closer to the subject so size grows because the camera walks. It is a short pressure advance, often so gradual the audience feels the walls close before they notice motion.

items.title: Pull Out
items.description: A pull out shot moves physically or virtually away from the subject so more environment enters around a person or detail. Intimacy widens into context without changing lenses.

items.title: Static Locked-Off
items.description: A static locked-off shot plants the camera on a heavy tripod with zero camera movement. Composition, blocking, and duration do the work; the frame is a living picture that does not tour.

items.title: Dolly Zoom
items.description: A dolly zoom combines camera movement and opposite zooming to preserve subject size while distorting perspective. It is not a zoom with a digital background stretch: translation and focal length work against each other.

items.title: Dutch Roll
items.description: A Dutch roll rotates the camera around the lens axis over time, so a level horizon becomes a canted one. Unease arrives as a move, not as a frozen Dutch still.

items.title: Camera Roll
items.description: A camera roll rotates the frame around the lens axis as if the world has lost its up, either by rolling the camera or by rotating a room around a weighted body. Gravity becomes optional, which is stronger than a small Dutch cant.

items.title: Double Dolly
items.description: A double dolly shot moves performer and camera together on one rolling platform so their relative arrangement stays fixed. The actor appears to glide rather than walk: feet skating, weight transfer absent.

items.title: SnorriCam
items.description: A SnorriCam fixes the camera to the performer's body so the body remains stable relative to frame while the world moves. A rig points back at the wearer: the face stays pinned, the environment pitches around it.

items.title: Locked-On
items.description: A locked-on shot keeps one object or face glued in frame while the world streams past, as if the camera were bolted to a vehicle, a fall, or a spinning set. The subject is the only stable point.

items.title: Walk and Talk
items.description: A walk and talk shot moves with speaking people, camera leading or flanking at medium, so information and geography travel together. Architecture flows while a moving two-shot (or a moving single with interruptions) carries the dialogue.

items.title: Hyperlapse
items.description: A hyperlapse combines time-lapse with significant camera movement through space. Time is compressed while the camera advances in steps that assemble into a glide, so crowds and weather race along a real path.

items.title: Slider Shot
items.description: A slider shot is a short, precise linear move on a compact rail, often 60 to 120 centimeters. It adds parallax to an interview, product, or lock-off without a full dolly track.

items.title: Lazy Susan
items.description: A lazy susan shot rotates the subject on a motorized turntable while the camera stays put, or the camera circles at a fixed product-hero radius. Distance holds, so scale does not change, and the far wall barely shears if the disc is what turns.

items.title: Bolt Cam
items.description: A bolt cam hurls an ultra-high-speed camera along a crash rig toward an impact, then freezes. The punch is physical translation on a rail or pneumatic throw, not a change of focal length.

items.title: Aerial
items.description: An aerial shot views a large area from a high flying camera so geography reads as a map, the figure small in land or city. Helicopter, drone, or a virtual path can carry it; altitude and a stable horizon are the facts.

items.title: Arc
items.description: An arc shot moves the camera around the subject along part of a circle while the lens stays aimed at them. A quarter or half orbit is enough: the axis of the scene changes without a cut, and the background slides.

items.title: Choreo
items.description: A choreographed camera times bodies and lens as one phrase of movement. The blocking is scored: steps, turns, and the support share a count, then the phrase ends.

items.title: Conveyor
items.description: A conveyor camera treats the world as a belt: relentless lateral travel at constant speed, factory or infinite product-line geometry. The subject can stand still while the line delivers the next unit past the frame.

items.title: Dolly
items.description: A dolly shot places the camera on a wheeled platform so the body translates through space: doorway dolly, Fisher, Chapman. Because the nodal point moves, foreground, mid-ground, and background change in parallax, which a zoom cannot do.

items.title: Falling
items.description: A falling camera drops the lens through air with weight and wind, a body or viewpoint in free fall. Gravity is the path: the ground rises, air rushes, and the horizon may not stay polite.

items.title: Fixed Cam
items.description: A fixed camera locks position and tilt so all motion belongs to the world, not the operator. The mount does not pan, tilt, or travel; blocking has to finish the shot.

items.title: Omnidirectional
items.description: Omnidirectional capture uses a 360 camera to record spherical space, so the viewer can look any way and there is no behind the camera. Off-screen ceases to exist as a hiding place.

items.title: Pan
items.description: A pan shot rotates the camera horizontally around a fixed position, yaw on the vertical axis, feet planted. The support does not travel; the horizon should stay level as the frame sweeps the world.

items.title: Parallax
items.description: Parallax cinematography is the relative apparent motion between near and far objects as the camera translates. Near things race, far things crawl; that speed difference is how the image proves the world has layers.

items.title: Pass Through
items.description: A camera pass through travels through a wall, a body, or a window as if matter were optional. The path is continuous: one side of the barrier, its thickness, then the next space, without a cut.

items.title: Tilt
items.description: A tilt shot rotates the camera vertically around a fixed position, pitch on the horizontal axis, tripod planted. Height is revealed or hidden by angle, not by lifting the support.

items.title: Trucking
items.description: A trucking shot is a lateral dolly: the camera slides sideways with a walker, a sidewalk or corridor peeling by. Subject size holds; the world streams along the street axis.

items.title: Wandering
items.description: A wandering camera drifts near the subject as curiosity, a search without a target yet. The move is not a motivated reframe to a known fact; looking itself is the action until something is found.

items.title: Zoom
items.description: A zoom shot changes focal length without moving the camera. Space flattens or opens with no parallax: near and far grow or shrink together because the nodal point stays put.

items.title: Eyes In
items.description: An eyes in camera push travels into the gaze until the irises own the frame. It does not stop at a close-up; the portrait becomes an interior of sclera, iris, and catchlight.

items.title: Mouth In
items.description: A mouth in camera move enters speech or appetite until lips and teeth become the set. The camera travels past the portrait into the orifice as landscape.

items.title: Eating Zoom
items.description: An eating zoom is a crash into the bite, chopsticks or spoon as the last foreground, appetite as a punch-in. The move is optical and short; the dish should be nameable in the last frame.

items.title: Buckle Up
items.description: A buckle up camera straps the lens to the cabin with the subject, so the vehicle is the tripod and acceleration is the grammar. Interior stays sharp; the world streaks past the glass.

items.title: Car Chasing
items.description: Car chase cinematography covers pursuit from a second vehicle, matching speed, the road as the set. Two machines stay in a line of action; this is the hunter's lens, not a locked interior.

items.title: Car Grip
items.description: A car mount camera bolts to hood, door, or bumper so bodywork sits in the near plane and asphalt slides underneath. Chrome and road share one rigid relationship because the rig is the machine.

items.title: Road Rush
items.description: A road rush camera sits low to the asphalt, speed as smear, headlights and lane lines as weapons. The road is the subject; a vehicle is optional.

items.title: Flying Cam Transition
items.description: A flying cam transition is one continuous flight that punches a wall or window and lands in a new room. Architecture becomes a tunnel; the join is travel, not a hidden cut.

items.title: Through Object In
items.description: Through object in sends the camera into a cup, keyhole, speaker, or mouth, matter as a door, then arrives on the subject. Scale often changes along a coherent 3D route that a physical camera could not take.

items.title: Through Object Out
items.description: Through object out leaves the subject by traveling out through an object into a wider world, interior becoming exterior. The viewpoint can abandon the person and let the decisive event happen off its direct attention.

items.title: Super Dolly In
items.description: A super dolly in is a long aggressive travel that eats the room, parallax violent, the face arriving too fast. It is a dolly in stretched until geography collapses into a close-up in one move.

items.title: Super Dolly Out
items.description: A super dolly out is a long retreat that dumps the person into geography, the room exploding open. The environment takes the frame; the figure is left inside a system they no longer fill.

items.title: Dolly Zoom In
items.description: A dolly zoom in approaches on wheels while the lens zooms out, so the figure holds or grows as the background warps inward. Counter-zoom is the point: size and space disagree.

items.title: Dolly Zoom Out
items.description: A dolly zoom out retreats on wheels while the lens zooms in, the figure shrinking or holding while space yawns. The background stretches away; the face can stay as the room leaves.

items.title: YoYo Zoom
items.description: A yoyo zoom inhales and exhales on the optical axis: a punch then a release, camera body still. One breath, two directions, no dolly.

items.title: Rapid Zoom In
items.description: A rapid zoom in snaps focal length faster than a polite crash, almost a cut, the world tightening in a few frames, then a hold. The camera body does not travel.

items.title: Rapid Zoom Out
items.description: A rapid zoom out snaps from the subject to a wide, the environment exploding into view, then holds. Reveal as shock or joke; the camera body still does not travel.

items.title: Head Tracking
items.description: A head tracking camera glues the lens to the skull so the face stays pinned while the background orbits. The head is the tripod; turns shear the room.

items.title: Hero Cam
items.description: Hero cam is a low three-quarter tracking walk with rim light, a comic-book arrival at walking speed. The recipe is height plus travel plus a hard edge of light, not a static low angle.

items.title: Robo Arm
items.description: A robotic camera arm runs a programmed path with inhuman precision, repeatable every take for product geometry or a stunt match. No operator shake; the spline is the performance.

items.title: Wiggle
items.description: A wiggle camera rocks between two nearby viewpoints, a tiny stereo fidget that makes a lock-off read as a living postcard. Travel is centimeters, not a dolly.

items.title: 3D Rotation
items.description: A 3d rotation camera treats the figure as a sculptural object on a virtual turntable of space. The world may be a cyc or a void; the point is every side, not a street orbit.

items.title: Crane Over The Head
items.description: A crane over the head rises on the arm until the camera looks nearly straight down, a person becoming a map. The end state is overhead, not a high three-quarter.

items.title: Earth Zoom
items.description: An earth zoom is a continuous or apparently continuous rush from satellite scale down to a face, continent to street to person. Nested geography collapses along one axis; a smooth zoom is not proof of real travel speed.

items.title: Jib Down
items.description: A jib down camera is a short descending arm, a few feet of boom, intimate arrival with nearby foreground sliding as the camera sits down. It is a small crane, not a city-scale drop.

items.title: Jib Up
items.description: A jib up camera is a short rising arm that gives a table or face back to the room, human-scale lift. Who else is present appears; a skyline does not have to.

items.title: Extreme Close-Up (ECU)
items.description: An extreme close-up, or extreme close up shot, fills the frame with one small feature: an eye, a mouth, a fingertip, a trigger. Surrounding space disappears; the crop is tighter than a whole face.

items.title: Choker Shot (BCU)
items.description: A choker shot, also called a big close-up (BCU), frames the face from hairline to chin, often clipping the skull on every side. Shoulders are out; almost no background remains.

items.title: Close-Up (CU)
items.description: A close-up, or close up shot, frames a face tightly enough to privilege detail over surroundings, usually head and upper shoulders. The room becomes secondary; the person still reads as a head, not a fragment.

items.title: Medium Close-Up (MCU)
items.description: A medium close-up, or medium close up, usually frames a person from chest or shoulders upward. Dialogue distance remains: face, shoulders, and often a hand at chest height stay readable.

items.title: Medium Shot (MS)
items.description: A medium shot frames a person from approximately the waist upward, so face and gesture share the rectangle. It is the workhorse size of coverage, sometimes called a waist shot.

items.title: Cowboy Shot
items.description: A cowboy shot frames a person from mid-thigh or the knees upward so the hands stay in at the holster line. It is also called an American shot or knee shot; it is not a waist shot and not a full figure.

items.title: Full Body (WS)
items.description: A full body shot holds a person head to toe, with the figure complete and a readable strip of environment around the silhouette. The person is still the subject; the world is a border, not the owner of the frame.

items.title: Long Shot (WS)
items.description: A long shot in cinematography shows the full subject plus a substantial portion of the environment, so a person sits small in geography. The figure is still locatable as a human; the world is large enough to ignore them.

items.title: Extreme Long Shot (ELS)
items.description: An extreme long shot makes environment, scale, geography, or isolation dominant over individual detail. A person, if present, is a speck: a scale mark, not a portrait.

items.title: Establishing Shot
items.description: An establishing shot introduces or re-establishes location, geography, time of day, or social context. It is a job in the sequence, not a synonym for wide or extreme long shot.

items.title: Master Shot
items.description: A master shot covers the complete dramatic action and the spatial geography of a scene in one setup. It is the skeleton you can play in full, then cut into.

items.title: Two-Shot
aliases: Shared frame instead of isolated faces
items.description: A two-shot, or two shot, frames two principal subjects together so their distance and posture can be compared in one composition. The space between them is part of the sentence.

items.title: Three-Shot
items.description: A three-shot, or three shot, frames three principal subjects together, usually so alliances and the odd one out are readable in the blocking. It is a group sentence of three, not three singles cut together.

items.title: Group Shot
items.description: A group shot frames a small ensemble as a relational unit, such as a family, a crew, or a jury. Position, height, and light say who belongs and who dominates.

items.title: Insert Shot
items.description: An insert shot is a close view of a story-relevant detail: an object, a hand action, a screen, or text. It points at the thing that will matter, at real scale.

items.title: Cutaway
items.description: A cutaway shot leaves the primary action for a related detail, observer, or part of the same world. It is used for context, reaction, compression, or continuity repair.

items.title: Reaction Shot
items.description: A reaction shot shows a character's response to an event, a line, or an unseen stimulus. The important action is watching; the face (or body) is the cut.

items.title: Over-the-Shoulder Coverage (OTS)
items.description: Over-the-shoulder coverage, or an over the shoulder shot, puts a near shoulder or head in the foreground while the far face stays sharp. Paired reverses preserve relational space.

items.title: Single
items.description: A single, in single shot cinematography, is a coverage shot of one principal character, not a one-take scene. A clean single keeps other bodies out; a dirty single lets a shoulder or blur from the partner chew the edge without becoming a true over-the-shoulder.

items.title: Cut-ins
items.description: A cut-in, or cut in shot, moves from a wider view to a closer detail of something already present in that space, usually along the same axis. It proves a fact the wide cannot prove: the hands, the phone, the wound.

items.title: Gesture
items.description: Gesture cinematography sizes and times a shot around a discrete expressive body movement: a hand, a glance, a weight shift. The plot is in the motion, not in an object sitting still.

items.title: Interview
items.description: Interview cinematography is a talking-head setup: stable size, eyeline just off the lens, a listener implied. Someone is answering a question we often do not hear.

items.title: Product
items.description: Product cinematography lights and frames an object the way a portrait treats a face: hero angle, catalog clarity, controlled reflections. The thing is the subject, not a plot insert in a messy room.

items.title: Video Portraits
items.description: A video portrait is a sustained, simply covered study of one person: stable size, patient time, the face as the whole event. Duration is the intimacy; a person is enough.

items.title: Wide Shot (WS)
items.description: A wide shot shows the subject in full environment, with bodies small enough that place still speaks. It is environment-forward coverage: do not isolate yet.

items.title: Eye Level
items.description: An eye-level shot places the camera at the subject's eye height with a horizontal sightline and a level horizon. It is the default equal relationship: height and tilt assign no rank until you leave this setup.

items.title: High Angle
items.description: A high-angle shot looks downward at the subject from above eye level, an oblique pitch rather than a straight drop. More floor enters the frame, the figure occupies less of the rectangle, and the viewpoint reads as observation from above.

items.title: Low Angle
items.description: A low-angle shot looks upward at the subject from below eye level, so verticals converge and ceilings or sky take weight. The camera is not merely low; it is pitched up, and that pitch is what assigns monument or intimidation.

items.title: Bird's-Eye View
items.description: A bird's-eye view shot looks steeply or directly down from a great height so people and furniture become a map. Height, not just distance, is the point of view: life reads as a board game or a ritual seen from above.

items.title: Worm's-Eye View
items.description: A worm's-eye view looks sharply upward from ground level or below the subject, an extreme low pitch that collapses verticals inward. The subject is a tower and the camera is dust.

items.title: Overhead Top-Down
items.description: An overhead top-down shot looks nearly straight down at 90 degrees, flattening bodies and spaces into a graphic arrangement. Faces are scarce; silhouette, props, and the plan of the table or room do the talking.

items.title: Ground Level
items.description: A ground-level shot puts the lens almost on the floor, so boots, hems, wheels, and the dirt become actors. Height is the fact: the camera starts from the ground plane, whether it looks along the street or steeply up.

items.title: Dutch Angle
items.description: A Dutch angle rolls the camera so verticals and the horizon appear tilted. The cant is usually static: gravity's down is no longer the bottom of the frame, which is why the world reads as off its axis.

items.title: Point of View
items.description: A POV shot makes the camera function as a character's optical viewpoint: what they see at their eye height. The looker's head and shoulder stay out of the frame; we inhabit the look, not a seat behind it.

items.title: Profile
items.description: A profile shot places the camera at 90 degrees to the head so one ear, the jaw, and the nose read as architecture, with the look offscreen. It is a true side view, not a three-quarter face and not a stamped coin if the living head still breathes.

items.title: Three-Quarter Angle
items.description: A three-quarter angle turns the face about 45 degrees to the camera so both eyes remain visible and the far cheek recedes. It is the standard narrative portrait angle: dimensionality without a full front or a true side.

items.title: Reverse Angle
items.description: A reverse-angle shot views the same spatial relationship from the opposing side, completing the axis of a look, a dialogue, or a standoff. Geography flips; the 180-degree line is respected so screen direction still matches.

items.title: Trunk Shot
items.description: A trunk shot places the camera inside a car trunk or similar confined pit, looking up at the people who open it, with the lid and rim framing their downward looks. It is a located low viewpoint, not a generic look-up in a parking lot.

items.title: Hip Level
items.description: A hip-level shot sits the camera around belt or holster height so hands, gait, and weapons share the plane of focus. It is a height choice, usually with a level horizon: the hands will decide.

items.title: Shoulder Level
items.description: A shoulder-level camera sits slightly below the eyes, at the height of a walking companion. It is less formal than true Eye Level and less monumental than a Low Angle; the face is still the target, seen from the deltoid rather than the pupil.

items.title: First-Person
items.description: A first-person camera makes the lens function as a character's bodily viewpoint, with a body that owns it: hands entering the frame, breath, tools, locomotion. It is subjective seeing as continuous embodiment, not a single optical insert.

items.title: Fourth Wall
items.description: A fourth-wall look aims the subject's eyes into the taking lens, so the scene admits an audience. The camera is no longer an invisible observer; it is a person in the room, or the spectator the character has decided to include.

items.title: Object POV
items.description: An object-POV shot is the viewpoint of a tool, a ball, a bullet, a phone, or a vehicle: the prop has eyes. The camera is parented to that object, so the object stays stable in the frame while the world moves relative to it.

items.title: Incline
items.description: An incline is a slight camera roll, a gentle cant of the floor rather than a full Dutch angle. The horizon is a few degrees off true, enough to suggest slope or unease without declaring that the world has fallen over.

items.title: Three-Point Lighting
items.description: Three-point lighting, the basic three point lighting setup, places a key, a fill, and a backlight so a face is modeled from one dominant side, opened in the shadows, and separated from the background. The key is brightest and sets direction; fill and back exist only as ratios against it.

items.title: Key Light
items.description: A key light in key light cinematography is the principal source that sets the subject's dominant direction, shape, and exposure. Shadows fall away from it; every other light is measured against it.

items.title: Fill Light
items.description: Fill light reduces contrast or adds detail in areas the key does not reach, usually from the opposite side and at a lower level. It is a ratio tool, not a second sun.

items.title: Backlight
items.description: Backlight in backlight cinematography is light coming from behind the subject toward the camera, tracing edges and lifting the figure off the background. It may stay a thin rim or, in haze, become a visible shaft.

items.title: Rim Light
items.description: Rim lighting is a narrow edge of light, usually from a flagged backlight, that separates a subject from the background without opening the face. The highlight sits on brim, hair, and coat; flesh stays mostly dark.

items.title: Kicker
items.description: A kicker light is a relatively hard side-back accent on cheek, jaw, shoulder, or an object edge, placed behind and to one side of the subject. It is a slice, not a full wrap and not a hair-only rim.

items.title: Hair Light
items.description: A hair light is a small source behind and above the subject that lights only the top of the hair as a rim so texture separates from the background. The face stays on the key or in cooler shadow.

items.title: Eye Light
items.description: An eye light in eye light cinematography is a small frontal source used to put a catchlight in the irises or to lift the eyes a fraction without becoming a fill. The face can stay in shadow; the eyes remain human, not lamps.

items.title: High-Key Lighting
items.description: High-key lighting, or high key lighting, uses relatively low contrast, bright exposure, and limited deep shadow so the frame stays open and readable. It is a contrast ratio, not a command to overexpose.

items.title: Low-Key Lighting
items.description: Low-key lighting, or low key lighting, uses high contrast, selective illumination, and substantial shadow so most of the frame can sit near black. One pool of light is often enough; the dark is designed, not an accident of underexposure.

items.title: Chiaroscuro
items.description: Chiaroscuro lighting uses strong light-dark contrast to model volume and to create moral, psychological, or dramatic tension. Darkness withholds; the lit plane is what the scene will admit.

items.title: Rembrandt Lighting
items.description: Rembrandt lighting, in rembrandt lighting terms, is a portrait pattern in which the key sits high and about 45 degrees off axis so the nose shadow joins the shadow cheek, leaving a small triangle of light under the shadow-side eye. The rest of that cheek stays dark.

items.title: Butterfly Lighting
items.description: Butterfly lighting, also called Paramount lighting, places the key high and on the camera axis so a small butterfly-shaped shadow falls under the nose on the philtrum. Both cheeks stay open; both eyes take light.

items.title: Loop Lighting
items.description: Loop lighting creates a small nose shadow that loops toward the corner of the mouth and does not connect to the cheek shadow. The key sits slightly off axis and a little high, a middle step between butterfly and Rembrandt.

items.title: Split Lighting
items.description: Split lighting divides the face into a lit half and a shadow half by placing the key at about 90 degrees to the nose, a vertical cut down the center line. There is no Rembrandt triangle and no loop; the far plane is largely gone.

items.title: Short Lighting
items.description: Short lighting in short lighting terms keys the side of the face turned away from camera, so the camera sees more shadow than light. The head looks slimmer and more dimensional because the near cheek falls off.

items.title: Broad Lighting
items.description: Broad lighting keys the side of the face turned toward camera, so the near cheek is the bright one and the shadow sits on the far side. The face reads open, public, and less mysterious.

items.title: Silhouette
items.description: A silhouette shot places the subject dark against a brighter background so the figure reads as shape, not as a modeled face. Gesture and contour do the work; surface detail is gone.

items.title: Motivated Lighting
items.description: Motivated lighting is designed to appear consistent with a visible or plausible story-world source: a window, a lamp, a sign, the sky. Hidden units may exist, but they match that source in direction, hardness, and color.

items.title: Practical Lighting
items.description: Practical lighting uses a visible or logically present light source within the set as a real contributor: lamps, neon, candles, screens. You see the fixture, and it (or a unit matching it) actually lights the face.

items.title: Available Light
items.description: Available light in available light cinematography is the illumination already at the location before the crew adds or changes units: sun, sky, or existing interior fixtures. You commit to the hour and the existing contrast.

items.title: Naturalistic Ambient
items.description: Naturalistic ambient lighting wraps the subject in soft, directionally plausible room or sky tone so the craft reads as unstyled even when units are added. Shadows stay believable; nothing announces a movie lamp.

items.title: Bounce Light
items.description: Bounce lighting reflects light from a surface (wall, ceiling, poly, card) before it reaches the subject, so the apparent source becomes that large surface. Direction remains, but shadow edges soften and wrap.

items.title: Hard Light
items.description: Hard light in hard light cinematography comes from a small apparent source and produces crisp shadow edges and specular definition on skin, metal, and walls. Texture is amplified; falloff can still be steep or long depending on distance.

items.title: Soft Light
items.description: Soft light in soft light cinematography comes from a large apparent source and produces gradual shadow transitions and wrap around the face or body. Speculars get larger and dimmer; texture is reduced.

items.title: Side Lighting
items.description: Side lighting keys primarily from one side, around 90 degrees to the camera-subject line, so shape and texture are emphasized. Half the form goes toward light, half toward shadow.

items.title: Top Light
items.description: Top lighting is illumination from directly above the subject, falling on forehead, nose bridge, and shoulders while the eye sockets and the underside of the chin go into shadow. The source is a ceiling, a rig, or a high practical, not a frontal beauty key.

items.title: Underlighting
items.description: Underlighting, also called uplighting, lights from below the face so shadows climb the cheekbones and the tops of the eye sockets. The modeling is the reverse of daylight and often reads as uncanny.

items.title: Cross Lighting
items.description: Cross lighting keys subjects from opposite side directions, so each person or each side of a body gets a key and a far rim. It is common in dialogue coverage, stage, and concert work.

items.title: Window Light
items.description: Window light in window light cinematography is illumination shaped to appear as light entering through a window: a large, directional source with falloff into the room. The architecture is the modifier.

items.title: Candlelight
items.description: Candlelight in candlelight cinematography is a small warm practical or a simulated flame with rapid falloff, often around 1800K, that carves faces near the flame and lets the rest of the room die. Flicker is part of the source, not a grade.

items.title: Neon Practicals
items.description: Neon practicals are visible neon or similar sign tubes used as actual keys or strong accents, coloring the subject with magenta, cyan, or other tube hues instead of a hidden white source. The city fixture is the lamp.

items.title: Golden Hour
items.description: Golden hour in golden hour cinematography is low-angle warm sunlight shortly after sunrise or before sunset, when the sun is near the horizon. Shadows go long; the light is directional, warm, and brief.

items.title: Blue Hour
items.description: Blue hour in blue hour cinematography is cool ambient twilight before sunrise or after sunset, when the sun is below the horizon but the sky still glows. There is no hard sunlight; the sky is a large cool source, and warm practicals often kick in.

items.title: Dappled Light
items.description: Dappled light is broken patches of brightness and shadow caused by foliage, water, blinds, or another irregular obstruction in a hard beam. The pattern is organic and often moving.

items.title: Gobo Lighting
items.description: Gobo lighting places a pattern or object in a light beam (a gobo or cucoloris) so the source throws graphic shadows across face, body, and wall. The room writes on the person.

items.title: Volumetric Light
items.description: Volumetric lighting makes beams visible through haze, fog, dust, smoke, or other particles, so the air photographs as well as the subject. Also called god rays or crepuscular rays when the shafts are distinct.

items.title: Cameo Lighting
items.description: Cameo lighting isolates a lit subject against a predominantly dark environment, so the figure sits in a pool and the world falls to black. The person remains modeled; the set is withheld.

items.title: Epiphany
items.description: Epiphany lighting is a change of illumination that makes a face or figure suddenly the brightest readable fact in the room as a realization lands. The light finds the person; it is timed to understanding, not left as a static setup.

items.title: Spotlight
items.description: A spotlight in spotlight cinematography is a focused, hard-edged pool from a theatrical or similar instrument, with darkness around the circle. The person is treated as an act inside that pool.

items.title: Glam
items.description: Glam lighting, in glam lighting terms, is a large beauty key with catchlights in the eyes and a little diffusion on skin, built to sell the face. It is a package of size, frontal or near-frontal placement, and skin treatment, not a single nose-shadow pattern.

items.title: Rule of Thirds
items.description: The rule of thirds in rule of thirds cinematography divides the frame into nine equal cells and parks important masses on those lines or at their four intersections. The horizon usually sits on an upper or lower third so land and sky are not equal partners, and the subject usually sits off-center with look-space in the larger remaining field.

items.title: Golden Ratio
items.description: Golden ratio composition organizes the frame with proportional relationships near phi, about eight to five, as a phi grid or a logarithmic spiral rather than a 3x3. The main mass sits closer to center than a third, and the eye is asked to travel a curve through secondary masses instead of jumping cell to cell.

items.title: Central Framing
items.description: Central framing, also called dead center or center punch, places the figure on the optical axis so the body sits on the crosshairs of the frame. Bilateral weight may gather around that body, but the first fact is placement: the person is the altar, not a guest in a third.

items.title: Centered Composition
items.description: Centered composition places the dominant subject on or near the central vertical axis and organizes the rest of the picture around that axis. The frame reads as a frontal tableau: walls, furniture, and attendants arranged so the subject is an altar, not an accident of blocking.

items.title: Symmetry
items.description: Symmetry in a symmetrical composition balances visual masses around an axis, usually the vertical centerline, so left answers right. The world looks designed, or it is pretending to be, whether or not a person occupies the middle.

items.title: Asymmetry
items.description: Asymmetry, or asymmetrical composition, offsets the dominant mass and answers it with a different kind of weight: color, light, a small face, a dark void, or a distant doorway. The frame does not mirror, so leftover space is a counterweight rather than a matching wing.

items.title: Leading Lines
items.description: Leading lines in leading lines cinematography are edges, rails, roads, corridors, shadows, or gestures that steer the eye toward or through the image. The lines are vectors in the diagram, not decoration around a centered face.

items.title: Frame within Frame
items.description: A frame within a frame (doorway framing, surcadrage) puts a second rectangle inside the screen, a door, window, arch, mirror, or gap that encloses the subject. The inner aperture is a second boundary, and crossing it is a beat, not a decoration.

items.title: Negative Space
items.description: Negative space in negative space cinematography leaves a large, relatively empty area around or beside the subject so absence becomes a mass. The unoccupied field is still a world (sky, wall, snow, sea), and the subject occupies a small or unusual portion of the diagram.

items.title: Foreground Interest
items.description: Foreground interest (a foreground anchor or occluded observation) puts a salient near object between the lens and the subject: flowers, a fence, glass, a table, or a body. The near layer creates depth, scale, a visual entry, or partial concealment, so air and obstacle sit between us and them.

items.title: Layered Depth
items.description: Layered depth, or layered composition, stages important action on at least two distances, typically foreground, midground, and background in one picture. Depth staging is that arrangement, while deep focus is a separate optical choice about how much of it is sharp.

items.title: Diagonal Composition
items.description: Diagonal composition uses diagonal lines and masses (stairs, rifles, rain, a body on the bias, a street receding on a corner) to raise energy, instability, or depth. The camera can stay level, because the set supplies the tilt of the diagram.

items.title: Triangular Composition
items.description: Triangular composition arranges subjects or visual masses into a triangle so three points lock the frame. A group gets a hierarchy: the apex is usually power, witness, or the object of desire, and the base is support, threat, or the audience inside the picture.

items.title: Headroom
items.description: Headroom in headroom cinematography is the space between the crown of the head and the top frame edge. Tight headroom applies pressure, while generous headroom hands the upper field to air, architecture, or sky.

items.title: Lead Room
items.description: Lead room in lead room cinematography (nose room, looking room) is space in the direction a subject looks or moves. More frame sits ahead of the walk or the gaze than behind the head, so the surplus is the path rather than leftover wallpaper.

items.title: Short Siding
items.description: Short siding places the face near the frame edge the character looks toward, crushing look-space and leaving surplus air behind the head. The edge they face becomes a wall, so the diagram denies them a future in the picture.

items.title: Visual Weight
items.description: Visual weight in visual weight composition is the attention an element attracts through size, contrast, color, position, focus, faces, or motion. A small bright thing can equal a large dark mass, because scale of attention is not scale of object.

items.title: Repetition and Pattern
items.description: Repetition and pattern composition repeats shapes, colors, lines, positions, or actions so the eye reads a system of columns, windows, soldiers, or hotel doors. A break in that pattern is often the story, because the grid had already set the expectation.

items.title: Figure-Ground
items.description: Figure-ground composition separates the subject from the field so the person or object reads in under a second. Contrast of tone, color, or focus does the split, and if figure and ground share the same value the diagram fails even if the acting is good.

items.title: Tonal Contrast
items.description: Tonal contrast, the contrast composition of lightest against darkest mass, organizes the frame as a fight of value with the subject as one of those poles. Graphic punch replaces mid-grey mush, so the diagram reads as a poster of value rather than a gentle range of detail.

items.title: One-Point Perspective
items.description: One-point perspective in one point perspective cinematography squares the camera to a plane so receding parallels meet at a single vanishing point, often on the central axis. The result is tunnel depth or ceremonial order: a corridor, a nave, a hotel hall aimed at infinity or at a person.

items.title: Vanishing Point
items.description: A vanishing point in vanishing point composition is the apparent meeting place of parallel lines in perspective, a destination for rails, a road, or a colonnade. The person often stands as a gate in front of that meeting, or occupies it as the target of the architecture.

items.title: Dirty Frame
items.description: A dirty frame in dirty frame cinematography lets out-of-focus shoulders, glass, foliage, or crowd chew the edges of the picture so the aperture is occupied. The camera sits inside a populated space, not on a seamless studio axis.

items.title: Clean Frame
items.description: A clean frame in clean frame cinematography keeps the edges empty of accidental objects so isolation arrives by tidiness, not by blur. The diagram has no landlord in the corners, which is studio-poster clarity even on a real street.

items.title: Look Space
items.description: Look space framing is the field in front of a gaze, the air a look owns, often because the important object is off-screen. In cutting, that look may be joined to what is seen (raccord regard, the look-object relationship).

items.title: Architexture
items.description: Architexture, a nickname for architectural cinematography that treats the set as subject, fills the frame with facades, grids, and materials until a person is a detail of the building. Texture, module, and mass own space, and the body is an ornament or a scale figure.

items.title: Reflections
items.description: Reflections in reflection cinematography put observer and observed in one plane by using glass, water, chrome, or a mirror. Mirror dialogue and one-way-glass staging let two spaces occupy a single composition, because optics, not a filter, do the doubling.

items.title: Screen in Screen
items.description: Screen in screen (desktop film, interface as the camera) nests a monitor, phone, television, or cinema inside the cinema so someone is watching a picture of someone. The inner image has its own crop, delay, and artifacts, and nested looking is the diagram.

items.title: Tableau
items.description: A tableau (tableau vivant, frontal ensemble, or frieze) is a staged composition whose meaning develops inside a relatively fixed frame. Arranged bodies and objects form a living picture, so duration replaces coverage while the camera stays locked or nearly locked.

items.title: Void
items.description: A void in void cinematography erases the set: darkness, white, or a blank field eating the world until a figure stands against nothing. Negative space still belongs to a place, while a void deletes place, leaving almost no landlord but the body or the darkness that might eat it.

items.title: Voyeur
items.description: Voyeur cinematography places the camera in concealment so the audience is trespassing: a view through foliage, glass, a grate, or a distant window, often with dirty edges. The diagram is a peephole, not coverage, and the owner of that hide does not want us there.

items.title: Windows
items.description: Windows cinematography treats panes as the true subject: stacked apertures, lives in rectangles, a building of frames. The diagram is a grid of possible pictures, not one doorway around one face.

items.title: 14mm Ultra-Wide
items.description: A 14mm ultra-wide in 14mm cinematography is a very short focal length that, from a close stand, takes in a huge field and exaggerates near-to-far size. The close camera position, not the millimeter stamp alone, is what balloons a foreground face or object against a receding room.

items.title: 24mm Wide
items.description: A 24mm wide in 24mm lens cinematography is a moderately wide prime that holds a person and a usable amount of place without extreme stretch. Body and architecture share the rectangle; neither fully wins.

items.title: 35mm Moderate Wide
items.description: A 35mm moderate wide in 35mm cinematography is the common narrative wide-normal: natural perspective with a little more world than a 50mm. It is default coverage for scenes that need both face and room.

items.title: 50mm Normal
items.description: A 50mm normal in 50mm cinematography is the conventional normal prime: from a typical stand it neither stretches near space nor stacks distant planes. The glass refuses to editorialize perspective; camera position still does all of that work.

items.title: 85mm Portrait
items.description: An 85mm portrait in 85mm cinematography is a short telephoto used from a farther stand so a head-and-shoulders stays large while the background enlarges and recedes in importance. The person becomes the landscape; the room becomes stacked color and shape behind them.

items.title: 135mm Telephoto
items.description: A 135mm telephoto in 135mm cinematography is a long lens used from a distant stand so planes stack and the background crowds the figure. The image feels like eavesdropping: you are far away, yet the world presses in.

items.title: 200mm Long Telephoto
items.description: A 200mm long telephoto in 200mm cinematography is an extreme long lens used from a very distant stand so size differences between planes almost vanish. Heat shimmer, stacked terrain, and sniper intimacy are the physical leftovers of that throw.

items.title: Anamorphic
items.description: Anamorphic cinematography squeezes one image dimension during capture, usually horizontally by 2x, then expands it for presentation. Depending on the lens, that cylindrical squeeze can produce oval bokeh, directional flares, and distinctive edge behavior; a wide aspect ratio alone is not anamorphic photography.

items.title: Spherical
items.description: A spherical lens in spherical lens cinematography uses rotationally symmetric elements with no anamorphic squeeze, so the image is captured already in its display proportions. Bokeh from a round iris is round, and edges stay rectilinear aside from ordinary wide-angle stretch.

items.title: Fisheye
items.description: A fisheye in fisheye cinematography is a very wide curvilinear projection that bends straight lines, especially away from the center. The world wraps around the lens; architecture becomes a bowl rather than a rectilinear box.

items.title: Tilt-Shift
items.description: Tilt-shift cinematography tilts the lens relative to the sensor so the plane of focus rotates, and may also shift the lens to slide perspective. A narrow band or shaped region of sharpness, often from a high viewpoint, can make a real-scale scene resemble a small model.

items.title: Macro
items.description: Macro cinematography is close-focusing optics that let a small object or surface occupy the image at high reproduction scale, often near 1:1. An unusually close view turns texture, insects, eyes, or mechanisms into the entire shot.

items.title: Probe Lens
items.description: A probe lens is a long, narrow macro optic that can pass through small spaces and create extreme close moving shots from inside the subject. The front element is tiny and far from the camera body, so the viewpoint can enter a glass, a wound of machinery, food, or a miniature set.

items.title: Split Diopter
items.description: A split diopter is a partial close-focus element that keeps different distance zones sharp in one frame. One region focuses very near while another remains focused farther away; it is not two focal lengths, and it is not ordinary deep focus.

items.title: Vintage Cine Glass
items.description: Vintage cine glass is older motion-picture optics whose coatings, contrast, and aberrations differ from modern clinical primes. Lower contrast, gentle halation, and sometimes swirling or rolling edges are properties of the lens, not a grade slapped on sharp digital.

items.title: Telephoto Compression
items.description: Telephoto compression in lens compression cinematography is the perspective effect of a distant viewpoint: size differences between separated depth planes shrink, so a crowd or a city appears to press against a person. A long lens then frames that distant view tightly; a long lens from a close stand does not create the effect.

items.title: Magnification
items.description: Magnification in magnification cinematography is the ratio of the subject's image size on the sensor to its real size. High magnification makes a centimeter of the world fill the frame; it is a scale number, not a shot-size name and not automatically a macro lens.

items.title: Teal and Orange
items.description: A teal and orange color grade pushes shadows and often skies toward cyan-teal while keeping skin and warm sources in the orange half of the wheel. It is a complementary split with faces protected, not a silver-retention process and not a general cool wash.

items.title: Bleach Bypass
items.description: Bleach bypass retains silver during processing, or simulates that retention, so the dye image sits on leftover metallic density. Contrast rises, grain shows, saturation falls, and highlights turn harsh rather than candy-colored.

items.title: Monochrome
items.description: Monochrome, including black and white cinematography, removes or does not record chromatic information so the image is value, texture, and shape. Hue is gone; contrast, grain, and outline do the talking.

items.title: Sepia
items.description: Sepia tone in sepia tone film maps the grey scale onto brown-gold instead of neutral silver, so whites go toward faded paper and blacks toward umber. It is a color of the past as chemistry, not a warm grade on a full-hue world.

items.title: Desaturation
items.description: Desaturation in desaturated cinematography reduces color intensity while leaving hue present. The world is wintered or dusted; leftover accents still speak, but chroma is no longer loud.

items.title: Hyper-Saturation
items.description: Hyper-saturation in saturated cinematography raises color intensity past ordinary record, so hues read as lacquer, fever, or dream. Feeling is louder than fact; the palette is not documentary.

items.title: Cool Blue
items.description: A cool blue grade in cool color grade work shifts the image toward steel, cyan, or moonlight blues across shadows and often midtones. Warmth, if it survives, is reserved for a practical or a face that the story wants to save.

items.title: Warm Amber
items.description: A warm amber grade in warm color grade work biases mids and highlights toward tungsten honey, candle, and practical glow. Safety, home, or nostalgia sits in the mids; the world is invited rather than chilled.

items.title: Filmic Faded
items.description: A filmic faded grade in filmic color grade work imitates a print: blacks are lifted off true zero, highlights roll off instead of clipping like video, and contrast sits like photochemical display. It is not HDR punch, and it is not automatically period costume.

items.title: Cross Process
items.description: A cross process look imitates developing a film in the wrong chemistry, such as slide stock in color-negative developer, so primaries skew off their true identities. Contrast often climbs; cyan shadows, magenta or yellow skin shifts, and other chemical accidents become the palette.

items.title: Day for Night
items.description: Day for night cinematography photographs daylight so it will read as nighttime while still showing terrain that true night might hide. Exposure, sky, and highlight control do the lying; a blue wash alone is not the technique.

items.title: Tungsten Balance
items.description: Tungsten balance in tungsten color temperature work sets the camera or stock for about 3200K so tungsten practicals render near-neutral or gently warm while daylight and cooler sources go blue. Different source colors remain visibly distinct rather than being normalized to one white.

items.title: Moonlight Gel
items.description: Moonlight gel in moonlight lighting gel work is a cool, often cyan or steel-green key standing in for the moon, usually a large source from above or through trees. Night stays sculpted: there is a direction, a rim, and deep underexposure, not only a blue grade.

items.title: Split Toning
items.description: Split toning in split toning cinematography assigns one hue to highlights and another to shadows, so the tone curve becomes a two-color world. Any pair is legal; teal-and-orange is only one famous instance.

items.title: Natural Grade
items.description: A natural color grade keeps skin faithful and saturation restrained so the location's real color science remains the authority. No stylized split, no silver punishment, no fever: the grade mostly refuses to editorialize hue.

items.title: Color Shift
items.description: A color shift effect is a change of color state that the audience is meant to notice: monochrome to hue, one world to another, or a slide of temperature during the shot. Color is the event, not a hidden LUT.

items.title: Vintage
items.description: A vintage film look treats the image as past chemistry: faded dyes, possible Halation, softened contrast, and period color that has drifted. It is a whole-file costume of time, not only old glass and not only a lifted print curve.

items.title: Palette
aliases: Palette as location or story state
items.description: A color palette in color palette cinematography is a restricted set of hues used as law across set, costume, light, and grade. Too many colors would be noise; a few chosen hues do all the work and can mark location, timeline, or story state.

items.title: Overexposed
items.description: Overexposed cinematography lets values clip or bloom toward white on purpose so information in the highlights is burned. It is a choice to lose the top of the scale, not the same as high-key lighting, which can stay bright while still holding detail.

items.title: Slow Motion
items.description: Slow motion cinematography plays action over more screen time than the event occupied during capture, usually by overcranking (recording 120 to 240 fps and playing at 24). The extra samples reveal fabric delay, particle hang, and impact mechanics that a 24 fps shutter would compress into a few smeared frames.

items.title: Fast Motion
items.description: Fast motion cinematography compresses screen duration so action plays faster than it occurred, by undercranking the camera or by retiming a normal-rate take. Crowds smear, clouds race, and labor can look absurdly efficient because too many events occupy too little time.

items.title: Speed Ramp
items.description: Speed ramping changes playback or capture speed inside a single shot rather than holding one retiming ratio. Approach and recovery stay energetic while one motivated instant (impact, glance, turn) stretches, then the clock returns.

items.title: Freeze Frame
items.description: A freeze frame holds one image so narrative time stops while camera, subject, and world all cease to generate new samples. The hold can end a story, land a joke, or present a face as evidence.

items.title: Time-Lapse
items.description: Time-lapse cinematography captures frames at long intervals so slow change plays as continuous motion, hours becoming seconds as shadows sweep and crowds become flow. It is interval photography, not a sped-up ordinary take.

items.title: Step Printing
items.description: Step printing repeats or omits frames optically or digitally so motion advances in visible temporal steps. Combined with low-rate capture and long exposures, each frame smears internally while the sequence stutters forward, a texture of delay rather than clean high-frame-rate slow motion.

items.title: Reverse Motion
items.description: Reverse motion plays recorded action backward so causes arrive after their effects inside the shot: rain rises, smoke inhales, a shattered object reassembles. This is reversed playback, not a story told in reverse scene order.

items.title: Bullet Time
items.description: Bullet time freezes or radically slows action while the viewpoint travels around it, decoupling camera speed from subject time. The instant becomes inspectable space: a time-slice orbit around a sculpture of speed, not ordinary slow motion with a handheld camera.

items.title: Long Take
items.description: Long take cinematography is an unusually extended shot that preserves continuous performance, space, action, or duration without an overt cut. Blocking and camera share one sentence so the audience cannot leave the room.

items.title: Oner
items.description: A oner shot is designed to play as if the scene were one take, with no visible edits. It may be a true single take or a stitched oner whose joins hide in whips, darkness, or crossing bodies.

items.title: Motion Blur
items.description: Motion blur cinematography is the streaking or softness caused by subject or camera movement during exposure. The longer the gate stays open relative to the motion, the more the image paints, so edges fail on purpose.

items.title: Stutter / Stop-Stutter
items.description: Stutter editing drops or repeats frames so playback skips and the world's clock hitches. It is an anxious rhythm, not the lyric smear of step printing and not a jump cut's spatial jump.

items.title: Boomerang
items.description: A boomerang video effect plays a short action forward, then snaps it backward along the same samples, often looping. The gesture comes and goes on one path: reversed playback used as a round trip rather than a one-way undo.

items.title: Infinite Loop
items.description: An infinite loop video sews the last frame to the first so motion never arrives at an ending. The cycle can be a seamless visual join, or, in narrative use, a repeated day whose variables change.

items.title: Stop Motion
items.description: Stop motion cinematography photographs physical objects incrementally, adjusting them between exposures so successive poses create apparent movement. The cadence is pose to pose and slightly staccato, with tactile materials in the light.

items.title: Low Shutter
items.description: Low shutter cinematography uses a short shutter angle or short exposure so moving edges stay sharp inside each frame. Normal-rate action then feels abrupt and staccato because this is reduced motion blur, not a long-exposure smear.

items.title: Timelapse Glam
items.description: Timelapse glam is interval photography of a styling process in which clothes, hair, and makeup change at high speed while the face holds. The person is a still axis and wardrobe is the changing weather.

items.title: Timelapse Human
items.description: Timelapse human holds one person in living time while the crowd is interval-sampled into smoke, so one still will stands in a rushing system. It is the opposite clock of a frozen world with a moving hero.

items.title: Timelapse Landscape
items.description: Timelapse landscape interval-samples light and weather over a place so hours play in seconds as clouds and shadows sweep. Geography is the actor, and a person, if present, is a scale mark rather than a racing extra.

items.title: Frozen in Motion
items.description: Frozen in motion stops the environment and most people while a chosen character, the viewpoint, or both continue to move. Particles, extras, and pigeons hang, and the rule of who may move is the entire effect.

items.title: Moonwalk
items.description: A moonwalk effect is a backward glide that reads as a forward myth: the torso stays upright, one foot slides, the other pushes, and the heel does not lift like a walk. It is a locomotion lie in living time, not reversed footage.

items.title: Lens Flare
items.description: Lens flare in lens flare cinematography is stray light scattered by glass, coatings, and barrel walls, producing ghosts, streaks, or veiling glare instead of a clean image. The artifacts live in the taking optic, so they track the source angle and dim when a body occludes the lamp.

items.title: Anamorphic Flare
items.description: An anamorphic flare is a horizontal streak produced when a bright point hits the cylindrical elements of an anamorphic lens. It is a subset of lens flare, not a general haze, and it usually arrives with oval bokeh from the same squeeze.

items.title: Halation
items.description: Halation in film is a reddish or warm glow around bright highlights caused by light passing through the emulsion, reflecting off the base, and scattering back into the image. It is a stock behavior, not a diffusion filter and not flare inside the lens.

items.title: Film Grain
items.description: Film grain in film grain cinematography is the random texture of silver halide crystals or color dye clouds in the emulsion, or a digital simulation of that structure. It is a developed surface, not a PNG overlay sitting on top of a clean render.

items.title: Bokeh
items.description: Bokeh in bokeh cinematography is the aesthetic character of out-of-focus rendering: the disc shape, edge, and smoothness of blurred points, not the mere fact of a thin depth of field. The glass, not a blur slider, decides whether those discs are round, oval, outlined, or swirling.

items.title: Double Exposure
items.description: Double exposure in double exposure film combines two or more image records on one frame, in camera by winding back, optically in a printer, or digitally as an additive composite. Both pictures occupy the same emulsion or file unless a matte fully holds one off.

items.title: Rack Focus
items.description: A rack focus moves the sharp plane from one subject or distance to another during a continuous shot, while the composition stays largely the same. Attention changes because the helical turns, not because the camera cuts or dollies.

items.title: Shallow Focus
items.description: Shallow focus keeps a narrow depth range sharp while foreground or background falls off. It is a depth-of-field choice made with distance, focal length, and aperture together, not a button labeled blur.

items.title: Deep Focus
items.description: Deep focus in deep focus cinematography keeps multiple near and far planes legibly sharp in one image. It is a continuous depth of field, not merely action arranged in depth while the glass stays selective.

items.title: Forced Perspective
items.description: Forced perspective uses camera position, subject distance, and set geometry to alter apparent size or distance, and the lie exists only from the taking viewpoint. Bodies, furniture, and eyelines must agree or the scale collapses.

items.title: Light Leak
items.description: A light leak in light leak film is unfiltered light that reaches the emulsion or sensor without passing through the taking lens, usually through a gap in the body, magazine, or gate. It fogs from the edge or along a scratch in the film path, often orange or red on color negative because it hits the base side.

items.title: Vignette
items.description: A vignette in vignette cinematography darkens, desaturates, or lowers contrast toward the frame edges because of optical falloff, mechanical vignetting in the barrel, a filter, or a later grade. Optical vignette follows the lens, while a post oval is a drawing.

items.title: Chromatic Aberration
items.description: Chromatic aberration in chromatic aberration cinematography is color fringing from different wavelengths focusing at different distances or magnifications. Lateral CA puts red-cyan (or similar) fringes on high-contrast edges, worse toward the frame edge, while longitudinal CA puts different colors in front of and behind the focus plane.

items.title: Infrared
items.description: Infrared cinematography photographs near-infrared reflectance (roughly 700 to 900 nm), not heat, so foliage often goes pale, skies go dark, and skin can look waxy. It is a different slice of reflected light, still a photograph of the location.

items.title: Night Vision
items.description: Night vision in night vision cinematography is image intensification: residual photons, and often a near-IR illuminator, amplified through a photocathode and microchannel plate onto a phosphor. The picture is typically green, grainy, blooming around lamps, with the framing of goggles, a weapon sight, or a camera in the dark.

items.title: Thermal
items.description: Thermal imaging cinematography maps emitted long-wave infrared (heat), not reflected light. A microbolometer or similar sensor assigns a palette (white-hot, black-hot, ironbow) to temperature, so faces, engines, and blood read warm while cold metal and night air do not.

items.title: Slit-Scan
items.description: Slit-scan exposes moving artwork or a moving camera through a narrow slit over time, stretching space into streaks and corridors with time laid along one axis. The result is structured geometry, not a random particle tunnel.

items.title: Kaleidoscope
items.description: Kaleidoscope cinematography fragments the image with mirrors or radial repetition so one subject becomes a symmetric pattern. The camera looks into angled glass, or the staging itself is a kaleidoscope: bodies arranged around an axis, often from above.

items.title: Light Flash
items.description: A light flash transition is a brief blowout of the frame to white or near-white, then a return, as if a bulb, explosion, or memory dump hit the emulsion. It is a temporal event, often a cut hidden in the peak, not a standing lens flare.

items.title: Projections
items.description: Projections in projection mapping film put a pictured image onto a surface that the taking camera then photographs: front projection onto a retroreflective screen, rear projection behind a window or windshield, or video mapped onto architecture. The projector is a light source, and the set is also a screen.

items.title: Morph
items.description: A morphing effect transforms one image, face, shape, or object into another by interpolating corresponding geometry over time. It is a continuous becoming, not a crossfade of opacities and not two exposures stacked.

items.title: Altered State
items.description: Altered state cinematography makes the mind the location: smear, afterimage, wrong color, unstable time, optics and cutting that no sober observer would report. It is a bundle of techniques motivated by consciousness, not a single filter name.

items.title: Anthropo
items.description: Anthropomorphic cinematography stages an object or animal as a performer: human scale in the frame, a gesture, an eyeline, reaction shots, as if the inanimate had a will. The camera does not need a face so much as an actor's grammar.

items.title: Cinemagraph
items.description: A cinemagraph is a still photograph in which one isolated element continues to move on a loop (steam, rain on glass, hair, a blink) while the rest of the frame is frozen. It is not a freeze-frame of a whole shot, and it is not a full clip that happens to loop.

items.title: Collage
items.description: Collage cinematography builds a frame from torn, cut, or mixed pieces: different stocks, paper, print, and live action sharing one plane with visible joins. Edges are graphic, and the stack is a construction, not an optical blend.

items.title: Datamosh
items.description: Datamosh is intentional codec failure: inter-frame prediction continues after keyframes are removed or broken, so motion vectors smear the previous picture into the next GOP and faces bleed into the following shot. The image is file wreckage, not a lens error.

items.title: Diorama
items.description: Diorama cinematography photographs a physical scale model so that it stands in for a much larger object or environment, with real light hitting real miniature surfaces. Scale is sold by texture, camera speed, depth of field, and movement, not by a toy-like tilt of focus.

items.title: Distortions
items.description: Lens distortion cinematography warps space so straight lines bow, stretch, or melt: barrel, pincushion, mustache, extreme wide stretch, or a physical distorting optic such as a diopter, a bottle, or rain on glass. The lens is lying about geometry, not adding flare.

items.title: Duplication
items.description: A duplicate subject effect puts the same performer in a frame more than once as solid bodies: twins, a self across a table, copies in one room. It is usually a split matte, motion control, or a locked-camera composite, not a translucent double exposure.

items.title: Echo Print
items.description: An echo print is an echo print effect that leaves a ghosted afterimage offset in time or register, so the last pose is still printed on this frame. The ghost is a stain of a previous exposure, not a second complete picture sharing the same plane.

items.title: Feedback
items.description: Video feedback is made by pointing a camera at its own live output so the picture nests into a recursive corridor of the same face. Each generation is a rephotograph of the monitor, with bloom, lag, and a tunnel of shrinking frames.

items.title: Floating UI
items.description: Floating UI, or HUD overlay cinematography, places readable interface, callouts, and data planes in the air of the scene so information lives in space, not only on a physical screen. The cockpit is the room.

items.title: Focal Shift
items.description: A focal shift moves the plane of sharpness from one subject or distance to another during the shot, so attention travels as a pull. The camera body can stay put, and only the focus mechanism walks the depth.

items.title: Generative
items.description: Generative visuals show process: forms grown by rule, particles, and iteration, so cinema is made by a system rather than only by a finished photograph. Making is visible.

items.title: Levitation
items.description: A levitation shot holds a body or object in a quiet impossible hover, refusing ordinary gravity while support is hidden or removed. Hair and cloth still hang, and the gap under the feet is the proof.

items.title: Masking
items.description: Masking cinematography uses a matte, a viewfinder object, or a graphic window so looking is visible as a shape cutting the picture. We see through binoculars, a keyhole, or a hard-edged hole.

items.title: Mixed Media
items.description: Mixed media film combines live action with type, illustration, and stock in one plane so no single capture method owns the truth of the frame. Media collide rather than dissolve into one photograph.

items.title: Morphing
items.description: Morphing cinematography transforms one shape or image continuously into another by interpolating geometry, rather than merely fading between pictures. Identity is a dissolve you can watch as contour.

items.title: Object Portal
items.description: An object portal effect treats a prop as a wormhole: a bag, a screen, or a doorway that should not lead there, opening onto another space. The thing is the cut.

items.title: Photogrammetry
items.description: The photogrammetry look reconstructs 3D geometry and texture from overlapping photographs, so a real place is turned into a scanned mesh. Slightly wrong normals, stretched texture, and holes are the evidence of capture.

items.title: Ratio Switch
items.description: An aspect ratio switch changes the image's visible boundaries so the container itself widens or closes as the story changes register. The picture is not stretched: previously unseen area is revealed, or the crop tightens.
