items.title: Scale Shift
items.description: Scale shift cinematography changes a body's size against the same room so the figure is suddenly giant or tiny: Alice physics as an optical event. Furniture, shadows, and contact have to match the new ratio.

items.title: Shadow Box
items.description: Shadow-box cinematography tells the story in layered cut-outs, depth as stacked silhouettes, a diorama of darkness. Figures are unfilled, and distance is paper stacked in front of a hard backlight.

items.title: Transformation
items.description: Transformation cinematography makes a body, room, or object become something else in continuous view. The camera keeps watching while the state changes, with a stable anchor so the becoming can be read.

items.title: Typography
items.description: Kinetic typography puts words in the world of the shot as objects: titles that occupy space, letters with scale, parallax, and a surface. The sentence is in the picture, not parked as a caption.

items.title: Wigglegram
items.description: A wigglegram is a short stereo shiver: two or three frames rocking so depth reads as a fidget. The viewpoints are a few centimeters apart, so depth is a twitch, not a dolly.

items.title: X-Ray
items.description: X-ray cinematography images through a surface as if denser structure were visible: bones, wiring, a body as diagram. Transmission, not reflectance, is the physics.

items.title: Zoetrope
items.description: Zoetrope cinematography shows the frames inside a movement: stroboscopic slices of a spinning action, motion as a drum of poses. You see the sampling, not a smooth blur.

items.title: Focus Change
items.description: Focus change cinematography jumps or slides the plane of sharpness to a new fact, a rack without apology. The mid-blur is short, and the new plane owns the shot as soon as it lands.

items.title: Floating Fall
items.description: A floating fall is a body hanging in a slow drop: delayed gravity on hair and coat, still going down. The path remains toward the ground, even when the clock on the body is late.

items.title: Smash and Grab
items.description: Smash-and-grab video is impact as coverage: glass, snatch, handheld chaos, a theft of a moment. The camera is inside the crime, too close and too late.

items.title: Cyclope
items.description: A cyclope camera is one giant iris looking: fisheye as a monster eye, a single hole, too close. The lens is the creature.

items.title: Particles
items.description: Particle effects cinematography fills the air with countable bits: dust, sparks, pollen, a weather of motes, each one catching light. Atmosphere you can inventory, not a blanket of fog.

items.title: Argus
items.description: An Argus image, argus many eyes, fills the frame with looking: extra pupils on a body, a swarm of viewpoints, a creature or a city of eyes. The surplus is seeing, counted as organs or cameras, not as flare.

items.title: Sticker Peel
items.description: A sticker peel effect lifts the image from a backing: adhesive shine, a die-cut layer coming off the world. Thickness, curl, and glue are the physics, not a still collage of torn paper.

items.title: Selfie Twin
items.description: A selfie twin puts two of the same face in a phone-arm frame, identity as a double take at arm's length. The camera is a compact wide in a hand, not a hidden studio body.

items.title: Bubbles
items.description: Bubbles cinematography fills the air with little lenses: soap films that refract the subject, rainbow edges, wet highlights. Each bubble is an optic, not a disk of bokeh.

items.title: Match Cut
items.description: A match cut joins two shots through a visual, spatial, sonic, or conceptual correspondence the viewer can read at the splice. The outgoing frame and the incoming frame share a shape, motion, object class, or idea, so the cut argues a relationship instead of only changing the view.

items.title: Graphic Match
items.description: A graphic match cut joins two images that share a dominant shape, line, color, placement, or motion pattern, even when location and time change. The outgoing contour and the incoming contour occupy the same part of the screen, so form carries you across the splice.

items.title: Match on Action
items.description: Match on action cuts during one continuous action so the movement itself bridges two camera positions. The outgoing shot starts the gesture; the incoming shot finishes it, which is why the edit can change size or angle without feeling interrupted.

items.title: Jump Cut
items.description: A jump cut removes time or slightly shifts framing inside a similar setup, so the discontinuity is conspicuous. The outgoing frame and the incoming frame are close enough that the missing interval reads as a skip, not as a new shot.

items.title: Smash Cut
items.description: A smash cut makes an abrupt, high-contrast transition in image, sound, tone, scale, or time. The outgoing side has earned a state (quiet, prayer, resolution); the incoming side contradicts it without a polite blend.

items.title: Dissolve
items.description: A dissolve gradually overlaps the outgoing shot with the incoming shot so both images occupy the frame for a measurable duration. Opacity of A falls as opacity of B rises; at the midpoint you are looking at two ghosts.

items.title: Fade In / Fade Out
items.description: A fade in or fade out takes the picture to or from a uniform field of black or color, rather than handing the frame straight to another visible scene. One side of the join is a world; the other side is absence, sleep, death, or a chapter break.

items.title: Wipe
items.description: A wipe replaces one image with another through a moving boundary that travels across the frame. One side of the join is still A; the other side is already B; the edge between them is the edit, and it is meant to be seen.

items.title: Iris
items.description: An iris transition reveals or conceals the picture with a moving circular or shaped mask. The mask's center is a pointer: one side of the join is the full world, the other is a hole closing on a face, a detail, or black.

items.title: Cross-Cutting
items.description: Cross-cutting alternates two or more locations or action lines, often implying they are happening at the same time. Each side of the join is a complete strand; the engine is meanwhile, two clocks racing.

items.title: Split Screen
items.description: Split screen shows two or more image fields at once, so separate spaces share a single moment on the same frame. Both sides of the join are visible together; there is no waiting for the next cut.

items.title: Montage
items.description: Film montage creates meaning or compression through the ordered juxtaposition of shots. Each side of a join is a complete image; the claim lives in the order, the collision, or the months squeezed into a minute.

items.title: Axial Cut
items.description: An axial cut jumps closer or farther along approximately the same camera axis, changing shot size without changing angle. The outgoing frame and the incoming frame share a viewpoint; only distance snaps.

items.title: Invisible Cut
items.description: An invisible cut hides an edit through motion, darkness, occlusion, blur, matching geometry, or digital stitching. One side of the join and the other are meant to feel like a single take; the splice is a seam the audience should not find.

items.title: J-Cut / L-Cut (Visual Setup)
items.description: A J-cut or L-cut visual setup is a picture designed so sound can lead or lag across the splice. One side of the join is a face, a room, or a listener that can hold; the other side is a space already speaking, or still speaking after we have left it.

items.title: Crash Cut
items.description: A crash cut slams two images together with no blend, so the join itself stings. One side of the splice and the other collide; unlike a smash that breaks an earned quiet, a crash cut often starts inside the event or hits like a drum from the first frame.

items.title: Flash Cut
items.description: A flash cut interrupts the present image with a few frames of another picture, then returns or races on before the insert can be studied. One side of the join is the ongoing scene; the other is lightning: a thought, a future, a wound, lasting a blink.

items.title: Match Motion
items.description: A match-motion cut continues direction and speed across the splice so the cut rides a vector even when location, time, or reality changes. One side of the join starts a movement; the other side keeps that movement, and the world around the body may be new.

items.title: Match Split
items.description: A match split continues a graphic line or motion across a divide, so one contour belongs to two worlds at once. One side of the join is a pane or half-frame; the other is its partner; the shared edge, horizon, or gesture is the match.

items.title: Quick Cuts
items.description: Quick cuts editing strings shots shorter than a breath, so duration itself becomes rhythm, pressure, or music. Each side of a join is a full view from a changing setup; the meaning is the rate, not a skip inside one frame.

items.title: Set Transition
items.description: A set transition lets the location change in camera: walls walk, architecture rewrites, one space becomes another without a hard cut. Both sides of the join are geographies that share a continuous camera path; the set itself is the editor.

items.title: Transitions
items.description: Film transitions are designed joins: the splice treated as a visible gesture rather than as continuity glue. One side of the join and the other are planned as a pair, and the audience is meant to notice how we left A and entered B.

items.title: Fragments
items.description: Fragments, or fragmented editing, build an event from partial views, so the audience infers an action more complete than anything shown in one shot. Each side of a join is a shard: a blade, a mouth, a drain, a hand too late; the whole lives in the gaps.

items.title: Rain
items.description: Rain in film is falling water that makes air visible as streaks and turns the ground into a mirror. Drops are matter in the optical path; without backlight they vanish, and without a wet-down the street stays dry under a fake storm.

items.title: Fog
items.description: Fog is a dense local suspension of water droplets that collapses depth, turns lamps into globes, and delays the reveal of figures. The air is matter close to camera; geography hides until someone walks into the last few meters.

items.title: Mist
items.description: Mist is a thinner water suspension than fog: pale layered air that still lets you read the next plane. Droplets are matter, but the veil is lyric, a morning or mountain breath rather than a wall.

items.title: Atmospheric Haze
items.description: Atmospheric haze is scattering over distance: far planes go paler and often cooler, so kilometers of air become the depth cue. The particles are too small to read as drops; the air is matter you measure in ridges, not in globes around a near lamp.

items.title: Smoke
items.description: Smoke is combustion particles with a source, a direction, and enough density to turn a room's air into a volume the light can strike. Unlike weather fog, it has a chimney, a cigarette, a tire, or a battlefield; backlight carves it into shafts and swirls.

items.title: Dust Motes
items.description: Dust motes are discrete particles hanging in a shaft of light, slow enough to read as time in still air. They are matter you can almost count; they live in the beam, not as a veil across the whole room.

items.title: Steam
items.description: Steam is water vapor released where heat meets colder air: trains, manholes, showers, a white veil that rises and thins. It is wet matter, not combustion; it billows, condenses on lens and wool, and has a thermal source.

items.title: Snow
items.description: Snow is ice falling and settling: large flakes in backlight, a muffled world, tracks that record who passed. The air holds crystals you can size; the ground accumulates; contrast goes soft because the world has been covered.

items.title: Wet-Down
items.description: A wet-down sprays pavement, asphalt, and cars so night lights double themselves in reflection, often with no rain in the air. The street is the effect; water is a surface treatment, not weather.

items.title: Sparks and Embers
items.description: Sparks and embers are incandescent particles thrown by welding, fire, grinding, or a cigarette: orange weather with short trajectories. They are burning matter; backlight is optional because they are their own small keys.

items.title: Dust and Sand
items.description: Dust and sand as weather is mineral grit driven by wind until the sun is a dull coin and figures become silhouettes. The land attacks: particles occupy near air, sting highlights, and erase the horizon that Atmospheric Haze would only pale.

items.title: Underwater
items.description: Underwater cinematography leaves air: the camera is in water, so caustics, buoyancy, and a missing horizon rewrite every edge. The medium is the matter; particles are silt and bubbles, and bodies move as if the world had gone slow without a slow-motion shutter.

items.title: Ocean
items.description: Ocean cinematography treats the sea as the other actor: swell, a horizon, salt light, a person against water that does not care. The atmosphere is spray, haze over distance, and a moving floor; the camera is in air, on a hull, or on rocks, not yet in the lung of the sea.

items.title: Film Noir
items.description: Film noir lighting is a low-key, high-contrast setup: a hard key, often cut by a venetian gobo or a streetlamp cookie, leaves one cheek in true black while wet pavement returns silver. The camera sits at eye height on a 35mm or 50mm spherical lens, tungsten practicals as motivated sources, and blocking that isolates a figure in a doorway, an alley, or a pool of light.

items.title: Neo-Noir
items.description: Neo-noir cinematography keeps noir's hard keys and isolated blocking but replaces silver night with color: sodium vapor, neon practicals, and tungsten that stain rain and skin. The camera still hunts faces in shadow, yet the palette is contemporary, often cyan signage against warm flesh, not black-and-white contrast alone.

items.title: German Expressionism
items.description: German Expressionism cinematography treats the set as a mind: forced-perspective corridors, painted shadows, and jagged hard light replace natural architecture. The camera is often locked and slightly dutch, so the actor walks a geometry that already looks illegal.

items.title: Giallo
items.description: Giallo cinematography is Italian thriller grammar: hyper-saturated primaries from gelled windows and glass, fashion interiors, and a camera that often zooms rather than dollies toward threat. Beauty lighting sits on the victim. The violence is styled, not silver.

items.title: Spaghetti Western
items.description: Spaghetti western cinematography restages western iconography on Techniscope 2.35: dusty ochre landscapes, hard sun as the only key, and cuts from a 24mm plaza wide to a telephoto extreme close-up of eyes. Moral ambiguity sits in the hold on a face before anyone draws.

items.title: Found Footage
items.description: The found footage look presents images as a recording made by someone inside the events, often later discovered or assembled, so the camera is a story object with a timestamp, a battery, and a reason to keep rolling. Consumer digital, Hi8, or MiniDV optics, autofocus hunt, and amateur framing are constraints, not decoration.

items.title: Cinéma Vérité
items.description: Cinéma vérité uses available light, zoom-to-find framing, and the filmmaker's presence as a catalyst, so the camera is admitted into the room rather than hidden. Unpretty 16mm or digital frames, mixed color temperature, and a zoom hunting the moment are the physical signature, not a recovered amateur tape.

items.title: French New Wave
items.description: French New Wave cinematography shoots fiction on locations with street light, handheld 16mm or 35mm, and an edit that will jump-cut rather than cover. The frame jumps into walking life: cafes, sidewalks, apartments with mixed practicals, and a camera that admits it is a camera.

items.title: Wuxia
items.description: Wuxia cinematography stages martial chivalry in landscape: misted bamboo or desert silk, long-shot geography, and wire-assisted paths that read as weightless rather than as street punching. Color is costume and fog, not a gelled murder window.

items.title: Tech Noir
items.description: Tech noir (also called future noir or cyber-noir) fuses noir's hard keys, rain, and guilty blocking with science-fiction production design: screens, LEDs, and corporate towers as practical sources. Analog crime grammar sits inside a digital city.

items.title: Southern Gothic
items.description: Southern gothic cinematography uses the American South as a humid optical problem: late-afternoon gold gone sickly, Spanish-moss Dappled Light, porch tungsten, and Atmospheric Haze that keeps heat in the air. Decay is on the walls. The threat is family, history, and something under the porch, not a city streetlamp.

items.title: Cosmic Horror
items.description: Cosmic horror cinematography builds dread from human insignificance: extreme long shots, slightly illegal geometry, under-light on faces, and a brightness that reveals too much. The threat is not a man. Scale, entity, and knowledge that will not fit a face are the optical problem.

items.title: Vaporwave
items.description: The vaporwave aesthetic is a pastel, low-contrast look: pink-cyan gradients, marble and palms, mall fluorescents, and VHS chroma bleed, as if a 1980s future never shipped. The camera is often centered and still. There is no crime geometry unless you add it.

items.title: Documentary
items.description: Documentary cinematography mixes observational coverage with interview and archive rhetoric: unstyled wardrobe light, mixed color temperatures, a zoom finding focus, and respect without a glamour rim. Fictional films may borrow the same grammar as mockumentary. That is still documentary rhetoric, not a recovered camcorder tape.

items.title: Blockbuster Gloss
items.description: Blockbuster cinematography is high-contrast, billboard-readable coverage: clean skies or designed weather, a heroic rim on hair and shoulder, volumetric shafts, and a grade that often splits teal shadow from warm skin. The shot must still parse at poster size.

items.title: Arthouse
items.description: Arthouse cinematography leaves space for thought: a Static Locked-Off camera, odd Headroom, natural or window light, and a frame willing to be empty. Duration is implied even in a still. The picture does not sell itself as a poster.

items.title: Animation
items.description: Animation cinematography constructs light and motion instead of capturing them: graphic volume, designed keys, and movement as drawing, paint, or stepped CG, not as a photographed exposure. The world is built. Lens physics appear only if you choose them.

items.title: BTS
items.description: Behind the scenes cinematography shows the making: C-stands, flags, the set wall, and crew in the same frame as the fiction, so the constructed world leaks. Documentary light (worklamps, mixed Kinos) sits beside the scene's key.

items.title: Dreamcore
items.description: The dreamcore aesthetic is a soft, liminal interior look: empty rooms, pools, and suburban halls lit by childhood practicals gone slightly wrong, with low contrast and unresolved space. Nostalgia is present. Safety is not.

items.title: Dystopian
items.description: Dystopian cinematography makes the civic system the antagonist: used architecture, haze, rank, and signage at a scale that already feels worn. The future is not shiny. It is bureaucratic, polluted, or monumental and cold, often in daylight as well as night.

items.title: Magical Realism
items.description: Magical realism cinematography treats an extraordinary event as ordinary inside a recognizable world: the same window light, the same 35mm coverage, with one impossible fact staged as if it were weather. The camera does not gawk, add a rim, or warp the lens.

items.title: Maximalism
items.description: Maximalist cinematography uses density as the point: too much color, too much pattern, ornament in every zone, and lighting that keeps the clutter readable rather than hiding it. Restraint would be a lie, so the frame is packed on purpose.

items.title: Photography
items.description: Photographic cinematography treats the movie as a print: a single decisive frame, posed or found light, often Centered Composition or Tableau blocking, with the camera pretending it could hang on a wall. Motion is allowed, but the still is the law.

items.title: Pixel Art
items.description: Pixel art builds the image from visible tiles or a low-resolution grid. The world is discrete squares, not continuous grain.

items.title: Stylistic Suck
items.description: Stylistic suck is deliberate amateur cinematography: hunting zooms, cheap video, and the wrong white balance as a choice of the film's own camera, not necessarily of a character's recovered tape. Polish would be dishonest, so the image is ugly on purpose.

items.title: Video Game
items.description: Video game cinematography uses playable camera logic: a follow cam, an isometric view, or an FPS eyeline, with space readable as a level and a HUD implied. Collision, boom height, and pathing constrain the lens the way a game engine would.

items.title: Weirdcore
items.description: The weirdcore aesthetic renders the familiar incorrectly: early-web compression, low-res sacred images, off-center crops, and a joke that is also a threat. The file looks like it should not have opened. Light is on-camera flash or a dim analog room, not a designed key.

items.title: Agamemnon
items.description: Agamemnon, the agamemnon look, is a named grade of hard sun, bronze bounce, and a dusk sky the color of a bruise, so a living body reads as antique metal. The name is not a shot: you still lock a height, pick a lens, and place a figure who can hold that weather.

items.title: Ink Riot
items.description: Ink riot, the ink riot effect, is liquid calligraphy occupying the air around a still-photographic subject: black and color blooming, dripping, exploding off a brush. The camera still needs a stand and a readable face, because the ink is weather, not a texture pack.

items.title: Fallen Angel
items.description: Fallen angel, the fallen angel look, is holy light after the drop: a shaft of dirty church air, low-key flesh, wrecked wings implied by cloth, shadow, or light. The face is the altar, and costume is optional.

items.title: Fairytale Castle
items.description: Fairytale castle, the fairytale castle look, puts storybook stone and impossible turrets around a small figure, with dusk treated as illustration. Place first, person second: the name is a location law, not a camera move.

items.title: Comic
items.description: Comic, in comic book cinematography, inks a live-action frame: hard edges, halftone in the shadows, limited spots of color, a page that still has a photographed body in it. The camera still has a lens and one sun, and it is not a screenshot of a book.

items.title: Cold Vision
items.description: Cold vision, the cold vision look, reads the world as temperature: either an arctic photochemical grade with breath and ice, or a thermal false-color overlay with heat edges. Empathy is not in the palette, so pick one sensor and keep it.

items.title: Casual Monster Slayer
items.description: Casual monster slayer is deadpan heroism in ordinary clothes: supermarket wardrobe, impossible creature work, the same naturalistic light on both. The joke is register clash, and the camera should look like coverage of a commute, not a poster.

items.title: Mighty Fighter
items.description: Mighty fighter, the mighty fighter look, is a living champion posed like cabinet art: oversized stance, hard rim, toy-box color, the city small behind them. It is a lock-off win pose, not a camera move and not motion blur.

items.title: Canvas
items.description: Canvas, the canvas painting look, is a photographic subject wearing oil: visible bristle, canvas tooth, thicker paint in the lights, eyes that still look. It is not a slider named oil: brushwork has direction and weight.

items.title: Pigeons
items.description: Pigeons, as a pigeons video preset, is a city takeoff: a stable person and a flock bursting as confetti, wings filling the air, then settling. The flock is the move, and the person is the hold.

items.title: Superstar
items.description: Superstar, the superstar look, is a face built for covers: beauty key, catchlights, a flash wall or crowd implied, wardrobe that photographs as money. Fame is a fact in the lighting, and the room is already looking.

items.title: Pearl Earring
items.description: Pearl earring, the pearl earring look, is a Dutch interior as grade: one north window, dark earth ground, skin like painted light, a small specular on a jewel. One window, one jewel, one look, and it is not a replica of a copyrighted painting.

items.title: LSD
items.description: LSD, the lsd visual look, is an optical state: light trails, slight double edges, oversaturated practicals, walls on a slow inhale. Perception is the set, not a scene of drug use and not a rainbow LUT.

items.title: Blue Depth
items.description: Blue depth, the blue depth look, stacks cyan planes so distance is a blue gradient: underwater, night glass, or air thick enough that the far plane goes deeper than the near. Depth is a color, not a cool white-balance wash.

items.title: Knight's Diary
items.description: Knight's diary, the medieval diary look, treats the frame as an illuminated page that still has mud on it: gold leaf as light, iron texture, dirt on cloth, a tired face like a saint who has been outside. It is period matter, not a plastic castle fair.

items.title: 2000s Paparazzi
items.description: 2000s paparazzi, the 2000s paparazzi look, is on-camera flash from a compact digital: greenish white balance, hard wall-shadow, sidewalk glare, a face not ready. Fame as a strobe: the theft is the lighting.

items.title: Dolphin Ride
items.description: Dolphin ride, as a dolphin ride preset, is impossible tourism played straight: a body mounted on a sea creature, bright water, honest horizon, splash readable. The gag is the vehicle, and swimming near a dolphin is not the sentence.

items.title: Multiverse
items.description: Multiverse, the multiverse look, puts the same person in parallel rooms, grades, and costumes at once, so one life is not the inventory. Versions must be separable: a double-exposure mush is not the recipe.

items.title: Skatedog
items.description: Skatedog, as a skatedog preset, is pavement grammar: camera near the deck or the paws, wide lens, asphalt in the foreground, a creature or rider in street sport as a joke. Keep it stupid and low, because standing height is the failure.

items.title: Sketch
items.description: Sketch, in sketch cinematography, is line on paper before paint: searching contours, hatching in the shadows, reserved paper in the lights, a drawing that still looks. Unfinished is the look, and a clean vector portrait is not.

items.title: Monet Muse
items.description: Monet muse, the monet look, dissolves a photographic scene into broken color: garden dabs, water as strokes, optical mix in the eye. Light is the subject, and defocus is not the same thing.

items.title: Akrill
items.description: Akrill, the acrylic paint look, is pigment as a plastic skin on the world: thick ridges, poster edges, high chroma, paint that still looks wet. Color sits on top: if it soaked in, you shot a wash.

items.title: Magazine
items.description: Magazine, in magazine cover cinematography, is a designed portrait with air for a masthead you will not render: fashion lighting, thumbnail-readable wardrobe, a page that knows it will be sold. Layout first, person second, and fake headlines will garble.

items.title: Lost in a Book
items.description: Lost in a book, the lost in a book effect, uses an open volume as a door: near-plane paper, a gutter as threshold, illustration or weather coming out of the page, a reader looking in or falling in. A person reading on a couch is not the recipe.

items.title: Penguin Ride
items.description: Penguin ride, as a penguin ride preset, is an absurd mount played straight: a person on a penguin through ice, slush, or the wrong city. The vehicle is the joke, and a penguin standing next to a person is not the sentence.

items.title: 3D Render
items.description: 3D render, the 3d render look, is a person as product visualization: clean global illumination, shader skin slightly too perfect, infinite cyc, contact shadows that never dirty. They should look computed, and photochemical grain is a joke if you add it.

items.title: Action Figure
items.description: Action figure, the action figure look, turns a person into merchandise: plastic joints, painted-on costume, blister-card studio lighting, a toy of a hero. Scale and material are the look, and a real actor in a costume is not enough.

items.title: Orbital Presence
items.description: Orbital presence hangs a body in vacuum over a planet: hard unfiltered sun, no air fill, a sharp planetary limb, the person as a satellite. Put them in orbit: a studio globe behind an actor is not the recipe.

items.title: Acid
items.description: Acid, the acid visual look, is a ruined print: burned chroma, melting edges, silver that shifted, dyes left in the sun too long. The dyes should misbehave, and a festive rainbow LUT is not damage.

items.title: Noir
items.description: Noir, the noir preset look, is wet streets, venetian gobos, and a crime already in the lighting: a motivated hard key, black pools, a face half-deleted. Night is moral, and a dark photo with teal is not this.

items.title: Race Track
items.description: Race track, the race track look, pins a body or a machine to circuit geometry: oval, painted curbs, catch fencing, grandstands, speed as a closed loop. The oval is the set, and a car on a generic highway is not the recipe.

items.title: Flash Comic
items.description: Flash comic, the flash comic look, is comic ink plus a strobe bang: inked edges, halftone, and a hard white burst, print and paparazzi in one hit. A panel that detonates: quiet comic ink without the flash is the cousin, not this.

items.title: Paper
items.description: Paper, in paper look cinematography, is the world as pulp: torn stock, visible fibers, a person as a cut-out on a page. The world is pulp, and creased lawful sculpture is origami, not this.

items.title: Random Glow
items.description: Random glow, the random glow look, is unmotivated orbs and analog leaks: a frame haunted by lamps that will not sit still. Optical accidents as style: even diffusion is the failure.

items.title: Toxic
items.description: Toxic, in toxic look cinematography, is air as contamination: sick greens, yellow haze, fumes you can backlight. The air is a hazard, and a teal grade with no particles is not poison.

items.title: Broken Mirror
items.description: Broken mirror, the broken mirror look, shards a person across cracked silver: one face that does not agree with itself, each shard a slightly different angle or time. Identity as a pile of cuts, and a crack overlay on a single face is not enough.

items.title: Hand Paint
items.description: Hand paint, the hand paint look, is wet strokes laid over a living picture, a painter's wrist still in the shot or at least a stroke that just happened. Canvas is finished oil; this is paint as a verb.

items.title: Lava
items.description: Lava, in lava look cinematography, is molten light: black crust, orange wounds, heat as the key from below, air that shimmers. The ground is still deciding, and an orange grade on a normal street is not geology.

items.title: Marble
items.description: Marble, in marble look cinematography, is stone as flesh: veined whites, cold polish, a statue that still breathes. They should look quarried: pale beauty skin without veins is not mineral.

items.title: Modern
items.description: Modern, in modern architecture cinematography, makes the room the thesis: glass planes, a designed void, a person small in Mies-or-Ando geometry. Production design first, and a loft with string lights is not this.

items.title: Puffin Ride
items.description: Puffin ride, as a puffin ride preset, is a commute on the wrong bird: a person mounted on a puffin against cliffs and spray, orange beak readable, played straight. A puffin next to a hiker is not the gag.

items.title: Origami
items.description: Origami, in origami look cinematography, is paper as lawful sculpture: creases, planar color, a person or city becoming a fold. The world folds, and torn pulp without crease law is paper, not this.

items.title: Two Color
items.description: Two color, in two color cinematography, is a duotone law: a pair of hues doing all the drawing, print as cinematography. Two inks, no extras: teal-and-orange with a thousand leftovers is not this.

items.title: Ultraviolet
items.description: Ultraviolet, the ultraviolet lighting look, is black-light cinema: a UV lamp as author, whites that scream, colors that only exist under that tube. The unseen made loud: a purple LUT on daylight is not a black light.
